name: Apache
info: The Apache are Southern Athabaskan-speaking peoples of the American Southwest, the Southern Plains and Northern Mexico, who call themselves Indé, resisted Spanish, Mexican and American invasion for centuries and live today in politically autonomous tribes.

facts.homeland: Apacheria: the mountains, valleys, canyons, deserts and southern Great Plains of what is now eastern Arizona, New Mexico, West Texas, southern Colorado and Sonora and Chihuahua; today tribes and reservations in Arizona, New Mexico, Texas and Oklahoma, among them Fort Apache, San Carlos, Mescalero and Jicarilla, and communities in Sonora, Chihuahua, Coahuila and Tamaulipas
facts.period: migration from the Athabascan homelands of the north into the Southwest between 1000 and 1500 CE (the history gives AD 1200 to 1500); first Spanish written record in 1598; raids on Sonora from the late 17th century; wars with Mexico and the United States in the 19th century; reservations from the 1870s; Geronimo's surrender in 1886
facts.known: six major groups: Chiricahua, Jicarilla, Lipan, Mescalero, Plains and Western Apache; wickiups and tipis; agave (mescal) as a staple food; the Sunrise Dance puberty ceremony of young women; the culture heroes Killer-Of-Enemies and Child-Of-The-Water; long resistance under leaders such as Mangas Coloradas, Victorio and Geronimo
facts.sources: Spanish accounts from Coronado in 1541 and Juan de Oñate in 1598; church baptism records studied by David M. Brugge; anthropologists such as Morris Opler, Grenville Goodwin and Keith Basso, working with Apache informants; archaeology of the Dismal River culture and the Cerro Rojo complex; linguistics from Harry Hoijer onward; census and Indian Affairs figures

t: The Apache speak languages of the Athabaskan family, related to that of the Navajo, and came into the Southwest from the north several centuries before the Spanish arrived.
Each Apache tribe is politically autonomous; historically the six major groups were independent of one another and sometimes fought each other.
After centuries of war with Spain, Mexico and the United States, and forced removals onto reservations, the Apache population has rebounded to 148,936 in the 2020 census.
dyk: Before the reservations, Apache families were mostly matrilocal: a married daughter's new dwelling was built near her mother's, and her husband joined her family, while among the Chiricahua a man avoided even the sight of his wife's female relatives.
ev: Francisco Coronado meets bison-hunting 'Querechos', possibly Plains Apaches, on the plains east of the Pueblos
Juan de Oñate makes the first known written record of the name Apache
The first Apache raids on Sonora appear to take place
Juan José Compà is killed for Mexican bounty money, and Mangas Coloradas becomes principal chief
The US Army forces about 1,500 Yavapai and Tonto Apache on a winter march to San Carlos that kills several hundred
An uprising against the reservation system begins Victorio's War
Geronimo's band surrenders at Skeleton Canyon and is sent to military confinement in Florida

sections.origins:
The Apache and the Navajo speak related languages of the Athabaskan family, whose other speakers live in Alaska, western Canada and on the Northwest Pacific Coast. Anthropological evidence suggests that the ancestors of the Apache lived in those northern lands before migrating to the Southwest, sometime between 1000 and 1500 CE by one reckoning and between AD 1200 and 1500 by another. Their mobile way of life, light dwellings and spare tools make their early sites hard to find and date, though substantial progress has been made since the early 21st century.

Scholars debate the route. One hypothesis brings them from the Great Plains and links them with the Dismal River culture, dated 1675–1725 and excavated in Nebraska, eastern Colorado and western Kansas. A competing theory sends them south through the Rocky Mountains, reaching the Southwest by the 14th century or earlier, and identifies an ancestral Apache assemblage there called the "Cerro Rojo complex". The two routes may both have been used, and archaeologists are finding ample evidence of a proto-Apache presence in the Southwestern mountains in the 15th century and perhaps earlier.

The name Apache comes from Spanish. Juan de Oñate wrote it first in 1598, and its origin is uncertain: the most widely accepted theory derives it from the Zuni word ʔa·paču, "Navajos", another from Yavapai ʔpačə, "enemy". Apache speakers call themselves Indé, "person" or "people". The six major groups are the Chiricahua, Jicarilla, Lipan, Mescalero, Plains and Western Apache.
sections.society:
All Apache peoples lived in extended families, each nuclear family in its own dwelling close to the others. An extended family was usually a husband and wife, their unmarried children and their married daughters with their husbands and children, so that it was joined through a line of women; a man moved into his wife's family at marriage. Sororate and levirate marriage were practised, and men avoided their wives' close relatives, most strictly among the Chiricahua. Several extended families formed a local group, led by a chief whose standing was not hereditary and whom no one was obliged to follow; the Western Apache looked for industriousness, generosity, impartiality and eloquence in a good chief. Local groups formed bands, most strongly among the Chiricahua and Western Apache.

Food came from hunting, gathering, farming, trade and raiding. Men mostly hunted deer, pronghorn, elk, bighorn sheep and, near the plains, buffalo, and a Mescalero hunter was expected to share as much as half his kill. Women gathered most plant food. Agave, or mescal, was the most important plant for the Chiricahua and Mescalero, its crowns baked in large underground ovens; the Western Apache gathered saguaro and prickly pear fruit, mesquite beans, acorns and pinyon nuts through the year. The Navajo farmed most, the Western Apache, Jicarilla and Lipan less, and some Chiricahua bands and the Plains Apache not at all.

Apache houses were tipis on the plains, wickiups in the highlands and earthen hogans in the deserts of northern Mexico. Among the Chiricahua the women built the dome-shaped brush wickiup and were responsible for it and everything in it.
sections.beliefs:
Apache religious stories tell of two culture heroes, Killer-Of-Enemies or Monster Slayer, of the Sun and fire, and Child-Of-The-Water or Born For Water, of water, the Moon and thunder, who destroy creatures harmful to humankind. Another tells of a hidden ball game in which good and evil animals decide whether the world should be forever dark. Coyote, the trickster, overturns social convention. The Navajo, Western Apache, Jicarilla and Lipan have an emergence or creation story; the Chiricahua and Mescalero do not.

Most Southern Athabascan gods are personified natural forces that run through the universe and can be used for human purposes through ceremonies. Keith Basso described the Western Apache concept of diyí' as a set of invisible powers derived from animals, plants, minerals, weather and mythological figures, which a person may acquire and use if they are properly handled. Medicine men learn the ceremonies, which can also come by direct revelation. Chiricahua and Mescalero ceremonies were mostly learned through personal visions, while the Jicarilla and Western Apache relied more on standard rituals. Important ceremonies include the puberty ceremony of young women, the Sunrise Dance, Jicarilla "long-life" ceremonies and Plains Apache "sacred-bundle" ceremonies.

Owls, snakes, bears and coyotes are considered spiritually evil and prone to cause sickness. Hunting was prepared with fasting and rituals; among the Lipan, deer were protected by the Mountain Spirits. Many ceremonies use masked representations of spirits, and sandpainting matters to the Navajo, Western Apache and Jicarilla. Dances for rain, crops and harvest sought to influence the weather and food supply.
sections.arts:
The Apache languages are the chief inheritance of the people's oral literature and ceremony. There are five Apache languages, all belonging to the Athabaskan branch of the Eyak-Athabaskan family, and all are endangered; Lipan is reported extinct. They are tonal and, unlike the Northern Athabascan languages, low-marked: stems that had a constricted syllable in the parent language took a low tone. Harry Hoijer divided them in 1938 into eastern and western branches, then revised his scheme in 1971, and other linguists such as Michael Krauss have found the relationships more complex. Kinship terms are rich: Chiricahua has four words for grandparents and uses the same terms reciprocally for grandchildren.

Influenced by the Plains Indians, the Western Apache wore clothing sewn from animal hides and decorated with seed beads, in linear designs resembling those of the Great Basin Paiute and bordered with narrow bands of glass beads in diagonal stripes of alternating colours. They made buckskin shirts, ponchos, skirts and moccasins with colourful beadwork.

Building was itself a craft. Morris Opler recorded the Chiricahua wickiup as about seven feet high and eight feet across, its frame of fresh oak or willow poles bound with yucca-leaf strands and thatched with bundles of bluestem or bear grass, with a smoke hole above a central fire and a hide at the door. Archaeologists have found the remains of such wickiups at sites such as Canon de los Embudos, where C. S. Fly photographed Geronimo's people in 1886. The Mescalero alone are known to use hundreds of different plants.
sections.exchange:
When the Spanish arrived, trade between the Pueblo peoples and the Southern Athabaskans was well established: the Pueblos exchanged maize and woven cotton for bison meat and hides. Spanish rule disrupted it, forcing the Pueblos to work mission lands, while the Apache quickly acquired horses. Spanish villages and Apache bands both raided and traded with each other for centuries. Apaches distinguished raiding, done by small parties for goods, from war, waged by large parties for retribution. The first Apache raids on Sonora appear to date from the late 17th century. The Lipan moved onto the Southern Plains before 1650 and were later forced into southern Texas and northern Mexico by the Comanche.

After Mexican independence in 1821, Mexico placed a bounty on Apache scalps by 1835. When Juan José Compà was killed for bounty money in 1837, Mangas Coloradas became principal chief and, with Cuchillo Negro, led retaliatory raids. After Texas statehood in 1846 the Americans waged a brutal campaign against the Lipan, destroying their villages. Mangas Coloradas made peace with the United States, but gold miners in the Santa Rita Mountains brought conflict in the 1850s, the Apache Wars.

The reservations forced bands with no kinship ties to live together, and many left them. In 1875 the US Army drove about 1,500 Yavapai and Tonto Apache 180 miles in winter from the Rio Verde reserve to San Carlos; several hundred died, and white settlers took their land. Victorio's War began in 1879. In 1886 Geronimo's band surrendered and was sent to confinement in Florida, and Apache children were later taken from their families for adoption by white Americans.
sections.legacy:
The Apache today live in tribes that are each politically autonomous. The federally recognised tribes include the Apache Tribe of Oklahoma (the Plains Apache, around Anadarko), the Fort Sill Apache Tribe, the Jicarilla Apache Nation of Dulce, the Mescalero Apache Tribe, the San Carlos, Tonto and White Mountain Apache tribes and the Yavapai-Apache and Fort McDowell Yavapai nations. After their release as prisoners of war, most Chiricahua joined the Mescalero and Lipan on the Mescalero Reservation, and the rest are enrolled at Fort Sill. In Mexico Apache communities live in Sonora, Chihuahua, Coahuila and Tamaulipas. The nine tribes formed the Apache Alliance, whose summits are hosted by each tribe in turn.

The population fell sharply in the 19th century. José de Urrutia estimated up to 60,000 Apache in 1700; there were 9,248 on reservations in 1875, and the census of 1910 returned at least 6,119. In the 20th and 21st centuries the population has rebounded, to 148,936 in the United States in the 2020 census. Modern Apache people use the Spanish name for themselves and their tribal affairs, and also their own term, Indé.

War with Euro-Americans left a distorted popular image. The anthropologist Keith Basso wrote that few peoples had been so consistently misrepresented, the image of "the Apache" spread by novels, histories and films being almost entirely "a product of irresponsible caricature and exaggeration". In early 20th-century Paris the word apache even came to mean an outlaw.

summary: The Apache are Athabaskan-speaking peoples who came south into the Southwest and Southern Plains several centuries before the Spanish, living by hunting, gathering agave and other plants, some farming, trade and raiding. They fought Spain, Mexico and the United States for centuries, endured scalp bounties, deadly forced marches and removals, and today live in autonomous tribes whose numbers have recovered.
references: Conrad, Paul (2021). The Apache Diaspora: Four Centuries of Displacement and Survival. University of Pennsylvania Press
Park, J. F. (1961). The Apaches in Mexican-American Relations, 1848–1861: A Footnote to the Gadsden Treaty. Arizona and the West, 3(2), 129–146
